title: Divine Foreknowledge and Human Responsibility in Salvation
english: If someone insists these events could not have taken place, we respond that they might not have occurred, but it does not follow that if something is incapable of happening, it must either happen or fail to happen; events unfold not solely by necessity, but also as contingent possibilities, including the possibility of non-occurrence. The examination of what is possible engages both logical analysis and reflective insight, enabling one who turns inward to perceive the subtlety of arguments and grasp how even fortuitous occurrences do not obstruct the potential for something to be actual in multiple ways—one of many possibilities becoming real, not by compulsion. God foreknew that events would unfold not through necessity but as free possibilities, and the declaration that they would occur is not speculative guesswork but genuine foreknowledge. Let no one suppose we have remained silent on predestination as if it were a heavy burden, for Paul affirms we know that all things cooperate for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose. Yet observe how the apostle immediately identifies the ground of this calling: those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be shaped into the likeness of his Son. Who, then, is more fitting for the righteous vocation grounded in God’s purpose than those who love him? Indeed, he makes clear the source of this calling lies within us—our purpose and foreknowledge: we know that all things work together for good for those who love God. For he nearly said that such cooperation occurs because those who love God are worthy partners in the good. At the same time, let us challenge those who speak contrary views and demand they answer us. Assume hypothetically that something depends on us; we will tell them they reject what depends on us until their argument collapses under the weight of the given hypothesis as unsound. Given that something depends on us, does God, by ordaining the sequence of future events, foreknow what will arise from what depends on us in each case where such dependence exists, or does he not? To claim he does not foreknow is to overlook the universal intellect and grandeur of God. But if they affirm he does foreknow, let us ask: is his foreknowledge the cause of what will come to pass, given that what depends on us exists? Or, since he foreknew, is foreknowledge entirely irrelevant as a cause of what depends on us? It was possible for some of these individuals, having answered otherwise, to have acted differently, and the self-determining creature brought into being could have chosen otherwise. In such discourses, the words 'Well done, good and faithful servant' are preserved, as well as 'You have been faithful over little; I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord.' Likewise preserved is the reasonable utterance of the wicked and slothful servant: 'You ought to have put my money to the exchangers.' Only justly spoken words will endure: to those on the right, 'Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,' because I was hungry and you gave me food, and what follows; but to those on the left, 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels,' because I was hungry and you gave me no food, nor what follows. Moreover, even if one were set apart for the gospel of God from the womb and had necessity imposed upon them, how could they consistently speak of subduing their body and leading into slavery if they had not yet been declared unapproved by others, and the woe would be theirs if they did not evangelize? Clearly, from this it follows that if they had not subdued their body and led into slavery, it would have been possible for them to be declared unapproved by others, and it was possible for woe to befall them had they not evangelized. Perhaps God both set them apart from the womb and for the gospel of God, together with perceiving the cause of the just separation: that they would subdue their body and lead into slavery, wary lest they themselves, while proclaiming, become unapproved; and knowing that woe would come upon them if they did not evangelize, they did not remain silent out of fear of God regarding the woe, but evangelized. And these things were seen by the one who set them apart from their mother’s womb and the one who set them apart for their own gospel: that there would be labors, imprisonments, beatings beyond measure, frequent deaths; by the Jews five times forty lashes minus one, three times beaten with rods, once stoned; and these things will happen to them.

title: Divine Calling and Apostolic Ministry
english: Boasting in trials and recognizing that trials forge endurance, and endurance—because of this, it was proper for him to be designated for God’s gospel, foreknown to exist and to be set apart from his mother’s womb. He was appointed to the gospel of God not due to any exceptional nature, nor because of superiority over other natures, but because of previously known deeds and later actions born of preparation and apostolic choice. At present, it was not fitting to deliver what is written in the psalm, for it would be digressive; thus, in the divine ordering, it will be given when we recount the psalm—this will be sufficient, even in excess, for the one who is set apart. For God is my witness, whom I serve in spirit through the gospel of his Son, as I continually remember you in my prayers, asking that I might at last come to you by God’s will, for I long to see you. Indeed, someone may come not according to God’s will, just as Balaam went to Balak, cursing Israel for hire; I also believe that every Gentile, or whenever the worship of God is foreign, not ministering to the beneficial holy things for them, does not prosper in God’s purpose to become toward those they approach, even if they thrive temporarily—what does scripture say about the evil prosperity of man? That I may impart to you a spiritual gift to establish you; this is indeed mutual encouragement among you through the faith you share, yours and mine. Regarding a gift that is not spiritual, I consider it necessarily follows: there are non-spiritual gifts, such as marriage, for the spiritual gift can never be hindered by prayer, yet the union of man and woman impedes it. The apostle indicates marriage as a gift when he says, ‘I wish all people were as I am,’ yet each has his own gift from God—one in this manner, another in that. I do not wish you to be unaware, brothers, that I often planned to come to you and was hindered until now, so that I might bear fruit among you, just as I have among other nations—Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish—and I am a debtor, so that my eagerness and you in Rome may preach the gospel. [But here is a parenthetical remark, which, if ignored, disrupts the sequence; for who would claim Paul was hindered from coming to the Romans in order to bear fruit? On the contrary, if he had not been hindered, he would have borne fruit; but being hindered, he was deprived of it—how then should we read? Often I planned to come to you that I might bear fruit among you, just as I have among other nations, Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish, and I was hindered until now; therefore, why was the parenthetical inserted? Because the purpose clause ‘that I may bear fruit’ was about to connect with much—for example, ‘that I also bear fruit among the other nations, Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish, I am a debtor, and the following’—so that it would not break continuity. Having inserted ‘I was hindered until now,’ he joined it to the former ‘I planned to come to you’ and the ‘that I may bear fruit,’ thus restoring the discourse’s order.] For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of people who suppress the truth in injustice. It also seems to be spoken of as wrath and the servant of those who have sinned laboring, and those under him of the same servants and ministers, as when God’s wrath was set to burn in Israel, when he caused David to rise against them, he commanded Joab to number the people; but the second stands from having sent out their wrath, anger, and tribulation, vengeance through evil angels. But then, those who labor through sin—I hear according to the allotment and unrepentant heart, he stirs up anger within himself on the day of wrath, and the fact that he has reached yet his anger to the end. Regarding these matters, consider whether the things happening to the righteous, when the evil one tempts them, wrath is indeed not from God nor from heaven, but from below somewhere, or from the devil or some of his angels; yet for these, no one plausibly argues that we are to wage war before the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, for these things will appear as those who are angry tearing apart the holy ones and bringing upon them wrath from heaven. title: Romans catena (u01-rem-close)
english: Just as what is lower has been revealed, so too does divine wrath from heaven rest upon us—though one might ask whether this wrath comes from heaven but not from God. If God has made truth known to all through the reasoning found in nature, and has revealed himself to each according to their capacity to complete that reasoning, then judgment must follow upon all ungodly and unjust deeds—more heavily for some, less for others—in proportion, so that the revelation of God’s heavenly wrath may be fulfilled. To those who, through steadfastness in good works, pursue glory, honor, and immortality, eternal life is given; but to those driven by rivalry, who reject truth while embracing injustice, wrath and anger, distress and anguish come upon every soul that does evil—first the Jew, then the Greek. Wrath is the punishment that follows sin; anger, they say, is wrath roused and made manifest, serving to convict when one suffers from sin—either through conscience being struck or through troubles that follow sin. Yet distress also follows such people, not from endurance itself, nor from fasting done for show, but only when it is bound up with anguish. No one would feel straitened if they had widened their heart like a snake’s girth and heard the apostle say, ‘Be widened, you also.’ For evil things tend to gather and narrow the soul, as the devil lies in ambush like a serpent. Glory, honor, and peace belong to everyone who does good—first the Jew, then the Greek—for God shows no partiality. Thus, the one who does good and valuable deeds, revealing their own worth, will receive honor by rising through repentance, from which they fell having become like senseless beasts; and having grasped what is worthy of immortality, they are raised in glory to eternal life. And in peace is everyone who is undistracted, not drawn aside by anything else to think or act against the truth, according to how God’s peace guards your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus—may peace be multiplied to you, and I give you my peace; and the prophet declares that peace will abound in the Lord’s visitation, so that false light, both by day and night, may cease to exist. For those who sinned without law will also perish without law, and those who sinned under the law will be judged by the law; for it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers who will be justified. Judgment comes according to law and through law, but destruction does not submit to law—nor does anyone else destroy them so that they may be judged by a law of destruction, but destruction holds those who sinned without law. Yet those who sinned under the law, not having utterly deserted it, whether by neglect or being overcome, yet still intending to live by it, will be judged by the law. With their conscience bearing witness and their thoughts accusing or excusing one another, on the day when God judges the secrets of humanity according to my gospel through Jesus Christ. [Or thus:] God judges according to the gospel, which is Paul’s gospel, and those who have made themselves worthy like him—among whom there is no sorrowful person, but only cause for joy—thus their gospel stands with God’s judgment as a minister entrusted with it. Therefore, the one who teaches something else about themselves, do they not teach themselves? The one who preaches against stealing, do they steal? The one who says not to commit adultery, do they commit adultery? The one who abhors idols, do they rob temples? The one who boasts in the law, yet transgresses it, do they dishonor God? For the name of God is blasphemed among the nations as it is written. Circumcision profits if you keep the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. One must inquire how often the law is spoken, especially by the apostle, so as not to appear to contradict oneself; at times when one is circumcised, Christ does not benefit you at all; at other times, circumcision helps if one practices the law. Thus the law is, in one sense, merely the letter of Moses; in its meaning, it has been said that if one is justified by the law, it is by grace that they have surpassed it—and the law has become our guardian until Christ.
